content: The Global Vector Control Response (GVCR) 2017–2030 highlights the significant global burden of vector-borne diseases. Approximately 80% of the world’s population is at risk of contracting one or more vector-borne diseases, which account for 17% of the global burden of communicable diseases. These diseases result in over 700,000 deaths annually. Vectors such as mosquitoes, flies, ticks, fleas, mites, lice, snails, and triatomine bugs transmit viruses, parasites, and bacteria that infect millions of people worldwide. Diseases caused by these vectors include malaria, dengue, leishmaniasis, Chagas disease, Zika virus disease, onchocerciasis, Lyme disease, plague, schistosomiasis, and yellow fever, among others. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a comprehensive strategy to strengthen vector control globally. This strategy was endorsed by Member States during the 2017 World Health Assembly, where a resolution was adopted to support its implementation. The strategy emphasizes an integrated approach to vector control, aiming to reduce the burden and threat of vector-borne diseases through effective, locally adapted, and sustainable interventions. Vector-borne diseases, once confined to tropical and subtropical regions, are now increasingly observed in temperate areas, causing outbreaks across all WHO regions. These diseases disproportionately affect impoverished populations, exacerbating poverty by hindering education, reducing work capacity, and limiting economic opportunities, such as tourism. The GVCR aligns with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and aims to contribute to achieving several Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including Goals 1, 3, 6, 11, 13, and 17. The strategy sets ambitious targets to reduce mortality from vector-borne diseases by at least 30% by 2020, 50% by 2025, and 75% by 2030, relative to 2016 levels. Similarly, it aims to reduce case incidence by at least 25% by 2020, 45% by 2025, and 60% by 2030. Key actions outlined in the strategy include enhancing vector surveillance, scaling up and integrating tools and approaches, and strengthening intersectoral collaboration. Countries are encouraged to revise their national strategic plans, define country-specific targets, and allocate necessary resources to re-align and strengthen vector control and surveillance programs. Community engagement is critical, with efforts to mobilize communities to eliminate vector habitats and improve housing conditions. Increasing the number of public health entomologists and ensuring adequate field and laboratory capacity are also essential components. The estimated global cost of implementing the strategy is $330 million annually, equivalent to about 5 cents per person at risk each year. This investment includes strengthening the workforce, improving coordination, and enhancing surveillance capacity. The allocation of resources is divided into vector surveillance (33%), coordination and planning (24%), and staff training (43%). Comprehensive vector control is the most effective approach to preventing vector-borne diseases. Millions of people have already benefited from vector control interventions, with significant reductions in diseases such as malaria, Chagas disease, and onchocerciasis. However, the full potential of vector control has not been realized or sustained for maximum impact on other diseases. The GVCR emphasizes the need for integrated, locally adapted, and innovative approaches to achieve long-term success in reducing the burden of vector-borne diseases globally.
